prompt: A Dataproc cluster of n2-standard-4 machines is up for an hour. What is billed for each machine?
hint: Whose machine is it, and what does Dataproc add?

choices.text: The Dataproc fee alone, which includes the machine
choices.why: The fee is $0.010 per vCPU-hour on top; the pricing page says the machine is billed by Compute Engine in addition.

choices.text: A DCU-hour for each processor
choices.why: DCUs are how Serverless bills; a cluster bills machines and the fee.

choices.text: The Compute Engine hour, its disk, and the fee on its four vCPUs
choices.why: Right: 0.30832 for the machine, 0.04 of fee and the boot disk by the GiB-hour.

choices.text: Only the Compute Engine hour, since Spark is open source
choices.why: Spark is free software, and Dataproc still charges its management fee for running it on your machines.

prompt: Match each role to what it runs.
hint: Only one kind of worker holds blocks of HDFS.
right_distractors: The Cloud Storage bucket the data lives in

prompt: A team keeps the only copy of its curated tables in the HDFS of a long-running cluster. What does that stop them doing?
hint: What happens to HDFS when its machines go?

choices.text: Reading the tables from Spark, which only reads gs:// paths
choices.why: Spark reads HDFS natively; the connector adds gs:// beside it rather than replacing it.

choices.text: Deleting the cluster between jobs
choices.why: Right: deleting the cluster deletes its disks and the blocks on them, so the cluster can never be disposable.

choices.text: Adding secondary workers to it
choices.why: Secondary workers can be added to any standard cluster; they simply hold no blocks.

choices.text: Running more than one job on it at a time
choices.why: YARN shares a cluster between jobs whatever the data lives in.

prompt: A cluster runs on image 2.2-debian12 and the team wants a newer Spark. What is the Dataproc way?
hint: What does an image version fix?

choices.text: Upgrade Spark in place with an initialization action
choices.why: Initialization actions run at creation; replacing the Spark an image was built and tested with defeats the image.

choices.text: Create a cluster on a newer image
choices.why: Right: the image fixes Spark, Hadoop and the rest together, so a new Spark is a new cluster.

choices.text: Ask for it with spark-submit --version
choices.why: That flag reports the version installed; it changes nothing.

choices.text: Run gcloud dataproc clusters update with the new image version
choices.why: A cluster keeps the image it was created on; upgrading means creating one.

prompt: A cluster is created with --num-secondary-workers=4 and no --secondary-worker-type. What kind of machines are the four?
hint: The help printed the default.

choices.text: Spot
choices.why: Spot is one of the three choices, and it has to be asked for.

choices.text: Non-preemptible standard VMs
choices.why: Non-preemptible is a choice you make; it is not the default.

choices.text: Preemptible
choices.why: Right: default="preemptible", as the command line said.

choices.text: The same type as the primary workers
choices.why: Secondaries share the machine type by default, and their provisioning model is preemptible unless told otherwise.

prompt: Mid-job, Google reclaims one of the cluster's Spot secondary workers. What happens to the job?
hint: What does a secondary worker store?

choices.text: It fails, because the HDFS blocks on that worker are gone
choices.why: A secondary worker runs no DataNode and holds no blocks; that loss belongs to a primary worker.

choices.text: The cluster is deleted with it
choices.why: That is what losing the master of a standard cluster does.

choices.text: It carries on, slower, with its tasks run again elsewhere
choices.why: Right: YARN gives the lost tasks to the machines that are left.

choices.text: It pauses until the worker comes back, then resumes where it stopped
choices.why: Nothing waits for the machine; the tasks are rescheduled at once.

prompt: In the autoscaling policy of the section, which statements are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Read the two Config blocks and gracefulDecommissionTimeout.

choices.text: The primary workers stay at two
choices.why: Yes: minInstances and maxInstances are both 2.

choices.text: A worker being removed may finish its tasks for up to an hour
choices.why: Yes: gracefulDecommissionTimeout is 1h.

choices.text: The policy reads CPU use from Cloud Monitoring
choices.why: It decides from YARN memory: what pending work asks for and what nobody uses.

choices.text: The secondaries can go down to none
choices.why: Yes: secondaryWorkerConfig.minInstances is 0.

prompt: An initialization action that downloads and compiles a library takes 25 minutes on every new cluster. What does the section suggest?
hint: Who pays for those minutes, and how many times?

choices.text: Raise --initialization-action-timeout to 30m
choices.why: The cluster would start, and every machine would still bill 25 minutes on every cluster.

choices.text: Build a custom image with the library on it
choices.why: Right: the cost is paid once, when the image is built, rather than on every cluster.

choices.text: Run the script only on the master, with the role check
choices.why: Any executor may run the code that imports the library, so the workers need it too.

choices.text: Keep the cluster running so the action only happens once
choices.why: That trades 25 minutes a night for 24 hours a day of machines.

prompt: What has to change in daily_orders.py for it to run on a Dataproc cluster instead of the laptop?
hint: Where do the paths come from?

choices.text: The master URL in SparkSession.builder
choices.why: The program names no master; spark-submit gives it one from outside.

choices.text: Nothing in the file: it is given gs:// paths as --src and --dst
choices.why: Right: the connector reads gs:// and the arguments carry the paths.

choices.text: The CSV reader, which cannot read from Cloud Storage
choices.why: Through the Cloud Storage connector, the same reader reads gs:// paths.

choices.text: The schema, since Dataproc infers types
choices.why: Spark behaves the same on both; the schema is written down in either place.

prompt: A downstream job starts as soon as a part- file appears under daily_orders/dt=2026-10-29/. What is the risk?
hint: What does _SUCCESS mean?

choices.text: Reading half a result, written by the tasks that finished first
choices.why: Right: each task writes its own part file, and _SUCCESS is what says all of them finished.

choices.text: Reading the .crc files as data
choices.why: Those are the local file system's checksums, and on gs:// they are not written at all.

choices.text: None: a part file is complete when it appears
choices.why: One part file can be complete while the others are still being written.

choices.text: Parquet cannot be read until Spark stops
choices.why: A finished Parquet file is readable at once; the question is whether all of them have finished.

prompt: With the master `local[2]`, Spark runs the job in one process with two ___ standing in for executors.
hint: Not machines, and not processes.

prompt: DuckDB counted 20000 orders in the CSV and 500 customers in the Parquet. On average, how many orders did each customer place that day?
hint: Orders divided by customers.

prompt: Which flag deletes a cluster after it has run no job for thirty minutes?
hint: The help listed it beside its stopping twin.

choices.text: --stop-max-idle=30m
choices.why: That stops the cluster and keeps its disks, which are still billed.

choices.text: --delete-max-age=30m
choices.why: That deletes it thirty minutes after creation, whatever it is doing.

choices.text: --delete-max-idle=30m
choices.why: Right: deletion after that much idleness.

choices.text: --initialization-action-timeout=30m
choices.why: That limits how long a boot script may run.

prompt: A workflow template uses managedCluster. What happens when it is instantiated and its job fails?
hint: The cluster belongs to the workflow.

choices.text: The cluster is kept so somebody can look at it
choices.why: The template deletes its managed cluster when the last job ends, succeeded or not.

choices.text: The cluster is deleted anyway
choices.why: Right: it is created for the workflow and deleted with it.

choices.text: The template retries the job on a new cluster forever
choices.why: A template runs its jobs once; retrying is the scheduler's decision.

choices.text: Nothing, because a template needs clusterSelector to create a cluster
choices.why: clusterSelector picks an existing cluster; managedCluster is the one that creates.

prompt: Match each shape to what it costs while there is no work.
hint: Which ones still have machines?

prompt: A cluster node costs 0.35654 USD an hour. What do a master and four workers cost for 3 hours, in USD, to two decimals?
hint: Five nodes for three hours.

prompt: A company inherits 120 Spark jobs and wants them on Google Cloud next month. Which choice does the lesson's reasoning favour?
hint: What does each option cost in work, not in dollars?

choices.text: Rewrite them in Beam for Dataflow, which is cheaper per hour
choices.why: Dataflow was the dearer of the three per hour here, and a rewrite of 120 jobs is a project.

choices.text: Dataproc, changing hdfs:// paths to gs://
choices.why: Right: existing Spark code is the largest reason Dataproc exists.

choices.text: One long-running cluster with no idle timer, sized for all 120
choices.why: Dataproc, yes, and the left-on line cost twelve times the ephemeral one.

choices.text: Keep them on premises, since no cloud engine runs Spark
choices.why: Dataproc, Serverless and Dataproc on GKE all run Spark.

prompt: Order these by the monthly cost of Quitanda's job as the program printed it, cheapest first.
hint: The cluster pays for its master; the batch for its driver.

prompt: A cluster has 2 primary workers and 40 Spot secondaries, and Spot capacity in the zone runs out mid-job. What is the likely outcome?
hint: Which machines are left, and do they hold anything lost?

choices.text: The job fails at once with lost HDFS blocks
choices.why: The secondaries held no blocks; the primaries that hold them are still there.

choices.text: Nothing changes, since the autoscaling policy replaces the lost Spot machines with standard VMs
choices.why: The policy adds secondaries of the type the cluster has; with no Spot capacity there is nothing to add.

choices.text: The work is carried by two workers, and the job takes far longer
choices.why: Right: nothing is lost, and almost all the processors are, which is why the section sizes secondaries as a share of the work.

choices.text: The master is reclaimed too and the cluster ends
choices.why: The master is a standard VM, which is the point of keeping it off Spot.

prompt: Left on all month, the cluster beats Dataflow above 22.5 hours of work a night. What does that say about a cluster used two hours a night?
hint: Which line is flat?

choices.text: It is cheaper than Dataflow, because the node is cheaper per hour
choices.why: Per hour, yes; left on, it pays 730 hours for 60 of work.

choices.text: It pays for about 20 idle hours a day, and --delete-max-idle is the fix
choices.why: Right: the guard is deleting it when idle, not a cheaper machine.

choices.text: It should move to larger machines to finish faster
choices.why: Finishing faster on a cluster left on does not shorten the hours it bills.

choices.text: Nothing: 22.5 hours is Dataflow's limit for a batch job
choices.why: It is a crossing of two prices, not a limit of any product.
